3.text: proceed to put the clothes on the body, which — considering that the body

4.text: is covered with a heavy skin, and that no part of it must be laid bare to

5.text: the gaze of those present — is a work of no little difficulty. At every hitch

6.text: in this task, the “followers” admonish the dead one, saying, “Leave off! make

7.text: haste! You have to go away. Do not be so obstinate!” The face of the

8.text: dead person is carefully covered over with the bib¹ of the fur shirt, and the

9.text: hood is drawn over and tied around the head. The belt of the man’s dress,

10.text: and a small piece of the collar-fringe of the woman’s combination-suit, are

11.text: taken off to be added to the household charms under the name of enaˊal.²

12.text: Some families, however, take simply a small piece of reindeer-skin and sew

13.text: to it a narrow strip of dog-skin. This represents a fur shirt trimmed with

14.text: dog-skin, and, by further association, the dead man himself. During the

15.text: preparations for the funeral this is added to the clothes of the dead spread

16.text: in the sleeping-room, as described before, and afterward taken off for the

17.text: household charms. It, also, is called enaˊal.

18.text: Divination. — After being dressed, the body is moved over to the

19.text: centre of the sleeping-room or to the outer tent, having its head, all the

20.text: time, directed to the exit; and the “fortifier,” or, less frequently, the nearest

21.text: relative of the deceased, proceeds to divining by the method of suspension.

22.text: This, for men, is done with a walking-staff, and for women, with the long

23.text: handle of a skin-scraper. The position of the body is the same as in the

24.text: similar process with living persons. The divinatory performance takes about

25.text: two hours, being repeated two or three times, at first in the inner room,

26.text: then in the outer room, and then again out of doors, before the entrance of

27.text: the tent. One of the first questions refers to the manner in which the body

29.text: For this the Chukchee generally have two methods, — either by burning

30.text: the body on a funeral pyre, or by carrying it away and leaving it on the

31.text: ground in the wilderness. Most of the Maritime people and of the reindeer-

32.text: breeders of the Chukchee Peninsula use, of course, the second method; while

33.text: the villages lying close to large accumulations of driftwood — as, for instance,

34.text: those on Cape Erri and also those of the reindeer-breeders of the Anui and

35.text: Anadyr — both burn and expose their corpses. Each family, however, uses one

36.text: and the same method from generation to generation. Thus a family in the

37.text: habit of burning its dead will, when solemnizing a funeral on the open tundra,

38.text: send two or three sledges to bring fuel from a distance of even thirty or

39.text: forty miles. Several pack-sledges will be taken apart and broken, and tent-

40.text: poles split up, to increase the size of the pyre. Nevertheless, the deceased
